flagged.urlStatus: 200, RFC 9110 #section-3.2 exists

flagged.problem: This is a strawman. Every web developer knows that a page or an API resource keeps its URL when its content changes, so nobody who studied would answer True. It teaches nothing about resources and representations.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer false, keeps the section at 6/6): "A tunnel reads and may rewrite the HTTP messages it relays between the two connections it joins." flagged.urlStatus: 200, RFC 9110 #section-3.7 exists
flagged.evidence: RFC 9110 §3.7 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-3.7): "A 'proxy' is a message-forwarding agent that is chosen by the client, usually via local configuration rules". The same section adds: "an 'interception proxy' ... differs from an HTTP proxy because it is not chosen by the client."
flagged.problem: The statement restates the RFC's definition of proxy, so it is a definition card. Read in everyday terms it is also open to dispute: transparent and interception proxies, which developers commonly call proxies, are not chosen by the client. The useful distinction is that a proxy is chosen by the client while a gateway acts as an origin server, and the card does not test it.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer true): "A gateway, also called a reverse proxy, acts as the origin server for the user agents that send it requests." Explanation: "A gateway acts as an origin server on its outbound connection and forwards requests inbound to other servers, unlike a proxy, which the client chooses." Same URL (§3.7: "A 'gateway' (a.k.a. 'reverse proxy') is an intermediary that acts as an origin server for the outbound connection").

flagged.urlStatus: 200, RFC 9110 #section-5.1 exists
flagged.evidence: RFC 9110 §5.1 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-5.1): "Field names are case-insensitive". However, RFC 9113 §8.2.1 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html#section-8.2.1) says a message containing uppercase characters in field names MUST be treated as malformed, and deck card sr11-03 teaches exactly that.

An HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 recipient does not treat Content-Type as equivalent to content-type: it rejects the message as malformed. An expert could answer False, and the card contradicts sr11-03. The prompt requires a card whose answer differs between versions to name the version it means.
flagged.suggestedFix: Pin the version (answer true): "In HTTP/1.1, a recipient treats the field names Content-Type and content-type as the same field." Explanation: "RFC 9110 defines field names as case-insensitive, so an HTTP/1.1 recipient matches Content-Type regardless of capitalization." Keep the §5.1 URL.

flagged.urlStatus: 200, RFC 9110 #section-5.1 exists

flagged.problem: The statement is a close paraphrase of that RFC sentence: the same structure and both exceptions, with only a few words changed. The prompt forbids this. The hedged "unless ... or ..." clause also marks the statement as true to a player who does not know the rule. It leaves out the contrast the section names: other recipients should ignore unrecognized fields.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer true): "A proxy must forward an unrecognized header field, while other recipients should ignore such a field." Explanation: "This rule lets HTTP be extended without updating deployed intermediaries; a field listed in Connection or blocked by configuration is the exception." Keep the §5.1 URL.

flagged.urlStatus: 200, RFC 9110 #section-4.2.3 exists
flagged.evidence: RFC 9110 §4.2.3 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-4.2.3): "The scheme and host are case-insensitive". The same section says: "HTTP does not require the use of a specific method for determining equivalence. For example, a cache key might be compared as a simple string", and "any HTTP component MAY perform normalization."
flagged.problem: "A client distinguishes http and https target URIs by the letter case of their host names" can be misread as distinguishing http from https by host case. More importantly, the RFC lets a client or cache compare URIs as plain strings without normalizing them, so a client may in fact treat EXAMPLE.com and example.com as different keys. An expert could defend True.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer false) with a statement about what the URIs identify, not about client behaviour: "The host names EXAMPLE.com and example.com in http URIs identify different resources." Explanation: "Scheme and host are case-insensitive in http and https URIs, and URIs equal after normalization can be assumed to identify the same resource." Keep the §4.2.3 URL.

verdicts.notes: I checked all 12 r1 cards against the downloaded RFC 9110 text. Every cited anchor exists and the page loads. RFC 9110 is the current Internet Standard and is not updated or obsoleted. Six cards pass: 04, 06, 07, 09, 10 and 12. Card 04 (reason phrase) is also backed by RFC 9112 §4 ("A client SHOULD ignore the reason-phrase content because it is not a reliable channel"), which would be the stronger URL because the card names HTTP/1.1. Card 06 does not depend on the comma versus comma-space question in reported erratum 9162. Card 09 correctly uses the server MUST 4xx rule, as distinct from a client's MAY discard. Card 10 matches §6.5.1 ("the trailers are simply discarded" and "a server SHOULD NOT generate trailer fields that it believes are necessary"). Card 12 matches §4.2.4 (MUST NOT generate userinfo) and does not repeat sr14-08. The replacements keep r1 at 6 true and 6 false: 02 becomes false, 03, 05 and 08 become true, 11 becomes false. Coverage gap: no r1 card tests the message parts (control data, header section, content, trailer section) beyond trailers. The tunnel replacement for 02 adds breadth on intermediaries instead.

flagged.urlStatus: 200 OK, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.3.1 (anchor present, RFC 9110 current, not obsoleted)

The answer (false) is right, but the false reason is the made-up phrase "standardized filter for the selected representation". Nobody who has studied HTTP believes the RFC standardizes GET content as a filter, so the card is a strawman. The misconception developers actually hold (that a GET body can change what the request means, as in Elasticsearch-style GET with a body) is left untested.
flagged.problem: Strawman wording: the false half ("standardized filter") is an invented claim no studied learner would accept, so the card does not test the real fact the prompt names: content in GET has no defined semantics and cannot alter the request's meaning or target.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replacement (answer false, keeps 6/6 balance): statement "RFC 9110 lets content in a GET request change the meaning or target of that request." Explanation: "RFC 9110 gives GET request content no generally defined semantics: it cannot alter the request's meaning or target, and some implementations reject such a request." Same URL.

flagged.urlStatus: 200 OK, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.2.1 (anchor present)

verdicts.notes:
I checked all 12 r2 cards (6 true, 6 false; average statement length 87.8 true vs 90.2 false). I opened every source URL (RFC 9110 §§9.2.1, 9.2.2, 9.3.1, 9.3.2, 9.3.3, 9.3.4, 9.3.7, 15.5.6; RFC 5789 §2; RFC 10008 §2). All return 200, the anchors exist, and each page supports its card.

These cards pass, with the quote that settles each:
- 02: "even if the original request succeeded, though the response might differ."
- 03: "A proxy MUST NOT automatically retry non-idempotent requests."
- 04: "The server SHOULD send the same header fields in response to a HEAD request as it would have sent if the request method had been GET." The card says "should", which matches the RFC's SHOULD.
- 06: "If the target resource does not have a current representation and the PUT successfully creates one, then the origin server MUST inform the user agent by sending a 201 (Created) response."
- 07: "Responses to POST requests are only cacheable when they include explicit freshness information ... and a Content-Location header field that has the same value as the POST's target URI."
- 08: "An origin server MUST NOT send a validator field ... in a successful response to PUT unless the request's representation data was saved without any transformation."
- 09: "The origin server MUST generate an Allow header field in a 405 response."
- 10: RFC 5789 says "PATCH is neither safe nor idempotent ... A PATCH request can be issued in such a way as to be idempotent." This matches the prompt's PATCH rule.
- 11: RFC 10008 §2 says "QUERY requests are safe with regard to the target resource."
- 12: "An OPTIONS request with an asterisk ("*") as the request target ... applies to the server in general rather than to a specific resource."

Minor points I did not flag:
- 06: the statement and explanation say "first representation", while the RFC's condition is "does not have a current representation". The card is still true, but "a current representation" would be more precise; a resource re-created after a DELETE also gets 201.
- 11: "even though" mildly signals True, but it is acceptable for a difficulty-1 QUERY card.

I found no duplicates with other sections. sr14-07 tests the fetch() TypeError for a GET body, which is a separate layer from sr2-05. sr6-04 and sr7-12 test different facts about PUT.

flagged.urlStatus: 200, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.5.10 loads and supports the card
flagged.evidence: RFC 9110 15.5.10: "The 409 (Conflict) status code indicates that the request could not be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the target resource." The statement restates the status name: a player who knows 409 is called Conflict can answer True from the wording alone, so the card tests a definition.
flagged.problem: Name giveaway and definition card: the statement says 409 means a conflict, which is the code's own reason phrase. Meanwhile 403, which the section plan pairs with 401, has no card.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace it with a true card. Statement: "An origin server may answer 404 instead of 403 to hide that a forbidden resource exists." Explanation: "RFC 9110 lets an origin server that wants to hide a forbidden target resource's existence respond with 404 (Not Found) instead of 403 (Forbidden)." Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.5.4 ("An origin server that wishes to 'hide' the current existence of a forbidden target resource MAY instead respond with a status code of 404 (Not Found)."). Answer stays true, so the 6/6 balance holds.

flagged.urlStatus: 200, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.2.1 loads and supports the card
flagged.evidence: RFC 9110 15.2.1: "The server intends to send a final response after the request has been fully received and acted upon." RFC 9110 15: "zero or more 'interim' (non-final) responses ... followed by exactly one 'final' response". The name "Continue" already says that more is coming.
flagged.problem: Strawman with a name giveaway: nobody who has studied HTTP would call a response named "Continue" final, so the false answer can be read from the name. The section's 100-continue and Expect fact can be tested with a misconception that people really hold.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace it with a false card. Statement: "A client that sends `Expect: 100-continue` waits for a 100 response before it sends any request content." Explanation: "RFC 9110 lets such a client send the content before any response arrives, and says it should not wait indefinitely, since a 100 (Continue) cannot pass through an HTTP/1.0 intermediary." Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-10.1.1 ("such a client MAY proceed to send the content even if it has not yet received a response"). Answer stays false.

flagged.urlStatus: 200, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-10.2.2 loads and supports the card
flagged.evidence: RFC 9110 10.2.2: "For 201 (Created) responses, the Location value refers to the primary resource created by the request." RFC 9110 15.3.2: "The primary resource created by the request is identified by either a Location header field in the response or, if no Location header field is received, by the target URI."
flagged.problem: Close to a truism: almost every web developer knows that Location on a 201 points to the new resource, and "201 Created" plus "Location" gives the answer away. The rule that teaches something is the fallback to the target URI when there is no Location.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace it with a true card. Statement: "When a 201 response has no Location field, the request's target URI identifies the primary resource created." Explanation: "RFC 9110 identifies the primary resource a 201 created by the Location field or, when no Location is received, by the target URI of the request." Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.3.2. Answer stays true.

verdicts.notes:
I checked all 12 r3 cards (6 true, 6 false) against the RFC text, which I downloaded and read directly: RFC 9110 sections 10.1.1, 10.2.2, 15, 15.2, 15.2.1, 15.3.2, 15.3.3, 15.3.6, 15.5.1, 15.5.2, 15.5.4, 15.5.5, 15.5.10, 15.5.16, 15.5.21 and 15.6.1 to 15.6.5, and RFC 6585 section 4. Every source URL returned 200 and is the right section. All 12 answers match the spec, and none needs a version pin.

The 9 cards that pass, with the sentence that settles each:
- 01: "treat an unrecognized status code as being equivalent to the x00 status code of that class".
- 04: 202 "is intentionally noncommittal".
- 05: "a server MUST NOT generate content in a 205 response".
- 06: the 401 sender "MUST send a WWW-Authenticate header field".
- 07: 404 "does not indicate whether this lack of representation is temporary or permanent".
- 09: the format problem might be found "as a result of inspecting the data directly".
- 10: 422 applies when "the syntax of the request content is correct".
- 11: RFC 6585 says 429 "MAY include a Retry-After header".
- 12: 502 means an "invalid response from an inbound server" and 504 means it "did not receive a timely response".

Minor notes, not flagged:
- 09: the explanation's phrase "rather than relying on its declared Content-Type" reads as exclusive. RFC 9110 lists the declared Content-Type or Content-Encoding and direct inspection as alternative causes. Acceptable, but "as well as from its declared Content-Type" would be more exact.
- 12: the source anchor points to the 15.6 introduction. The 502 and 504 subsections are on the same page.

Coverage gaps the replacements partly close: the section has no card on 103, 403, 407, 408, 410, 413, 414, 417, 428, 500, 503 or 505. The 403/404 replacement for card 08 and the Expect: 100-continue replacement for card 02 add two of those topics without breaking the true/false balance.

Duplicate check: I compared every card with the rest of the deck, including sr2-06 (PUT answering 201), sr4-05 (resolving a relative Location), sr14-01 (fetch() and 500) and sr8-05 (504 for only-if-cached). None of them rests on the same fact as an r3 card or as the proposed replacements.

flagged.urlStatus: 200, rfc-editor.org RFC 9110 #section-15.4.2 loads and supports the card
flagged.evidence: RFC 9110 15.4.2 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.4.2): "The 301 (Moved Permanently) status code indicates that the target resource has been assigned a new permanent URI and any future references to this resource ought to use one of the enclosed URIs." The answer is right, but 301 meaning a permanent move is among the most widely known HTTP facts. Nobody who studied would answer True to 'treat the new URI as a temporary replacement', so the card is a strawman.
flagged.problem: This is a strawman. Calling 301 a temporary replacement is a misconception no learner who studied would hold, so the card teaches nothing beyond the status name.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace and keep the answer false. Statement: "RFC 9110 says a client ought to use the Location URI of a 302 response for its future requests." Explanation: "A 302 means the resource resides temporarily under another URI. Because that can change, RFC 9110 says the client ought to keep using the original target URI for future requests." Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.4.3 ("the client ought to continue to use the target URI for future requests"). New factKey: found-target-uri-future-use.

flagged.urlStatus: 200, MDN Redirections #order_of_precedence exists, page last modified Aug 27, 2026
flagged.evidence: MDN (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Redirections#order_of_precedence): "HTTP redirects always execute first — they exist when there is not even a transmitted page. Somewhat surprisingly, JavaScript redirects execute next, before HTML redirects. This is because the <meta> redirect happens after the page is completely loaded, which is after all scripts have executed." The card is true, but it tests the self-evident half: a 3xx response is acted on before any HTML exists. The non-obvious fact MDN highlights is that a load-time JavaScript redirect runs before a <meta> redirect.
flagged.problem: Near-truism. HTTP redirects running before HTML redirects follows from the 3xx arriving before any page content, so a player can answer from common sense. The surprising, teachable fact about the order (JavaScript before <meta>) is not tested.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace and keep the answer true, volatility may_change. Statement: "MDN says a JavaScript redirect that runs while a page loads executes before an HTML <meta> redirect." Explanation: "MDN notes that a <meta> refresh redirect happens only after the page has completely loaded, after its scripts ran, so a load-time JavaScript redirect wins; HTTP redirects run before both." Same source URL.

verdicts.notes:
I checked all 12 r4 cards (b1 file). Every source URL returned 200, and each anchor exists: RFC 9110 sections 10.2.2, 15.4.1, 15.4.2, 15.4.4, 15.4.8 and 15.4.9; RFC 10008 section 2.5; Fetch Standard #http-redirect-fetch, last updated 6 October 2026; MDN #order_of_precedence.

Verified against the primary text:
- 02: 307 \"MUST NOT change the request method\".
- 03: 303 Location \"is not considered equivalent to the target URI\".
- 04: \"A 308 response is heuristically cacheable\". Note that \"Permanent Redirect\" in the statement nudges a guesser toward True. This is borderline, not flagged.
- 05: a relative Location is resolved \"against the target URI\".
- 06: a user agent MUST process the redirect as inheriting the fragment.
- 07: 300 lets \"the user (or user agent) select a preferred representation\". Small wording nit: 300 offers information about alternatives, not the representations themselves.
- 08: Fetch step: \"the moment another origin is seen after the initial request, the `Authorization` header is removed\".
- 09: 301/302 with POST become GET.
- 10: request-body header names are deleted when the method is rewritten.
- 11: RFC 10008 2.5: \"the exceptions for redirecting a POST as a GET request after a 301 or 302 response do not apply to QUERY requests\". Fetch only rewrites POST on 301/302, so the browser layer agrees.

No duplicates with other sections. r7-04 (404 heuristically cacheable) uses the same \"A cache classifies ... as heuristically cacheable\" template as r4-04, but tests a different status code. Both are true, so the false-template limit does not apply.

The section stays at 6 true and 6 false, and both replacements keep their card's answer.

Facts from the section scope that no card covers: RFC 9110's field removal/replacement list when following a redirect (Host, Referer, Origin, Authorization, Cookie), client loop detection (SHOULD), and the RFC-level MAY for POST to GET on 301/302. These could be used if more replacements are needed.

flagged.urlStatus: 200, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-12.1 loads (anchor present), official, current (RFC 9110 not obsoleted or updated)
flagged.evidence: RFC 9110 Section 12: ""proactive" negotiation, where the server selects the representation based upon the user agent's stated preferences"; Section 12.1: "When content negotiation preferences are sent by the user agent in a request to encourage an algorithm located at the server to select the preferred representation, it is called "proactive negotiation"". https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-12.1
flagged.problem: The answer is correct, but the statement just restates what the term "proactive negotiation" means: the server picking a representation from the request's preferences. That makes it a definition card, which the prompt bans ("a statement whose answer follows from the meaning of a term in it"). It is also a close paraphrase of the RFC's own definition.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer true). Statement: "In proactive negotiation, a server may also weigh the client's network address or User-Agent." Explanation: "RFC 9110 says proactive selection can use implicit request characteristics, such as the client's network address or parts of User-Agent, as well as explicit fields like Accept." Same URL (Section 12.1: "including both the explicit negotiation header fields below and implicit characteristics, such as the client's network address or parts of the User-Agent field").

flagged.urlStatus: 200, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-12.4.1 loads, official, current
flagged.evidence: RFC 9110 Section 12.4.1: "For each of the content negotiation fields, a request that does not contain the field implies that the sender has no preference on that dimension of negotiation." https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-12.4.1
flagged.problem: The statement is about what an origin server does ("An origin server treats an omitted Accept-Language field as ..."), not about what the missing field means. When a client expresses no preference, the server may serve any language, and many real servers do fall back to English. An expert could therefore defend True as a description of common server behaviour. The RFC fact is that the request expresses no preference. As written, the card is ambiguous and close to a strawman.
flagged.suggestedFix: Reword so the card tests what the request means (answer false). Statement: "Under RFC 9110, a request that omits Accept-Language signals a preference for English." Explanation: "A request without a content negotiation field, such as Accept-Language, expresses no preference on that dimension; the server may choose any language it holds." Same URL.

verdicts.notes:
I checked all 12 r5 cards: 6 true, 6 false. True and false statements average 94.0 and 90.2 characters, within the 5-character rule. Every card cites a section anchor of https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html. I downloaded the page (HTTP 200) and confirmed that each cited anchor exists (8.3, 8.3.1, 8.5, 8.7, 12.1, 12.4.1, 12.4.2, 12.5.1, 12.5.4, 12.5.5).

I checked the cards that pass against the RFC text:
- 01: \"The type and subtype tokens are case-insensitive\". The RFC lists Text/HTML;Charset=\"utf-8\" as equivalent to text/html.
- 02: \"the recipient MAY either assume a media type of \"application/octet-stream\" ... or examine the data\". The wording is close to the RFC sentence but restructured, and the prompt names this fact explicitly.
- 03: Content-Language \"might not be equivalent to all the languages used within the representation\".
- 04: Content-Location \"is not a replacement for the target URI ... It is representation metadata\".
- 06: \"determined by finding the media range with the highest precedence that matches the type\". The card does not depend on the last row of Table 5, so erratum 7138 does not affect it.
- 07: \"a value of 0 means \"not acceptable\"\".
- 09: \"the origin server can either honor the header field by sending a 406 ... or disregard the header field\".
- 10: order of equal-q tags \"cannot be relied upon\".
- 11: Accept in a response gives \"which content types are preferred in the content of a subsequent request to the same resource\".
- 12: Vary is \"a list of request field names\", and its purpose 2 is to tell user agents the response \"was subject to content negotiation\".

On the RFC 9110 errata search, the only 12.5.1 erratum is the Table 5 row (7138). The only 8.3.2 erratum is Accept-Charset versus Accept-Encoding (7419), which no r5 card uses.

I found no duplicates with other sections:
- sr1-05 (field-name case) is a different fact from sr5-01 (media-type case).
- sr7-05 and sr7-06 test Vary cache matching, while sr5-12 tests Vary as a negotiation signal.
- sr3-09 (415) is unrelated.

Coverage gap, not flagged: reactive negotiation, the default q=1 and Accept-Charset deprecation, all listed in the r5 scope, have no card. The suggested replacement for 05 keeps proactive negotiation; a reactive-negotiation card could replace it instead if broader coverage is preferred.

flagged.urlStatus: 200, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-8.8.3 loads (RFC 9110, current Internet Standard)
flagged.evidence: RFC 9110 8.8.3: "the origin server MUST mark the entity tag as weak by prefixing its opaque value with \"W/\" (case-sensitive)." The fact and the source are correct, but the statement pairs "weak entity tag" with "W/", so a player who knows nothing about HTTP can guess True from the letter W.
flagged.problem: Name/wording giveaway: W for weak can be read straight from the statement. The section's "Last-Modified implicitly weak" fact is untested anywhere in the deck (I grepped all four batches) and would replace it well.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer stays True). Statement: "An origin server treats a `Last-Modified` date in a request as a weak validator unless it can deduce that it is strong." Explanation: "RFC 9110 calls a Last-Modified time implicitly weak: with one-second resolution two changes can share a timestamp, unless the origin server reliably knows that did not happen." URL: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-8.8.2.2 ("A Last-Modified time, when used as a validator in a request, is implicitly weak unless it is possible to deduce that it is strong").

flagged.urlStatus: 200, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-13.1.3 loads and supports the right fact
flagged.evidence: RFC 9110 13.1.3: "A recipient MUST ignore the If-Modified-Since header field if ... the request method is neither GET nor HEAD." Also 13.1.3: the field "makes a GET or HEAD request method conditional". This is a field the client sends. The statement says "An origin server may use `If-Modified-Since` to make a PUT conditional".
flagged.problem: The answer (False) is right, but the statement names the wrong actor. An origin server never uses a request field to make a request conditional; the client does that. So the card is false for two reasons (wrong actor and wrong method), which breaks the one-clear-reason and name-the-actor rules. A player can also answer it correctly for the wrong reason.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (answer stays False). Statement: "An origin server evaluates `If-Modified-Since` on a PUT request before it applies the update." Explanation: "If-Modified-Since conditions only GET and HEAD, and a recipient must ignore it on other methods. A lost-update check for PUT uses If-Unmodified-Since or If-Match instead." Same URL (RFC 9110 Section 13.1.3).

verdicts.notes:

I checked all 12 r11 cards against my own copies of RFC 9113 and RFC 9110. Both were fetched from rfc-editor.org on 2026-10-08 (HTTP 200), and every cited section anchor exists. The RFC 9113 info page shows Proposed Standard, obsoleting RFC 7540 and 8740, with no newer RFC that obsoletes it.

The 10 unflagged cards and the sentences that settle them:
- 01: Section 5, "A single HTTP/2 connection can contain multiple concurrently open streams, with either endpoint interleaving frames from multiple streams."
- 02: Section 5.2.1 item 5, "only DATA frames are subject to flow control; all other frame types do not consume space in the advertised flow-control window."
- 03: Section 8.2.1, a field name MUST NOT contain 0x41-0x5a, and a message that violates this "MUST be treated as malformed". Section 8.1.1 lists "the inclusion of uppercase field names".
- 04: Section 8.3, "All pseudo-header fields MUST appear in a field block before all regular field lines."
- 06: Section 8.2.2, "An endpoint MUST NOT generate an HTTP/2 message containing connection-specific header fields. This includes the Connection header field ..."
- 07: Section 8.3.1, "Clients MUST NOT generate a request with a Host header field that differs from the \":authority\" pseudo-header field." The card's \"must\" matches this MUST.
- 08: Section 8.1.1, a request is malformed "if the value of a content-length header field does not equal the sum of the DATA frame payload lengths that form the content".
- 09: Section 3.2, "A client that makes a request to an \"https\" URI uses TLS with the ALPN extension. HTTP/2 over TLS uses the \"h2\" protocol identifier."
- 10: Section 9.1.1, connections "MAY be reused for requests with multiple different URI authority components ... as long as the origin server is authoritative". For https, reuse "additionally depends on having a certificate that is valid for the host in the URI". Chrome's extra IP-match check does not make the RFC's \"may\" false.
- 11: RFC 9110 Section 15.5.20, "A proxy MUST NOT generate a 421 response." The explanation's origin server or gateway wording matches the RFC. This card is borderline trivia: the more useful 421 fact for developers is that a client MAY retry, even a non-idempotent request, on a different connection. I did not flag it because the proxy rule is a real MUST NOT and a plausible misconception.

Balance and wording:
- The section has 6 true and 6 false cards.
- Statement lengths average 96.0 for true and 93.5 for false.
- Hedge words are balanced: can, must and may appear in true cards; may, can and may in false cards.
- None of the cards duplicates a card in another section. Cards 09 and 10 do not overlap the Alt-Svc cards in r12, and card 01 differs from r12's stream-independence fact.

Coverage gaps (breadth, not per-card defects): the r11 SECTIONS list names facts that no r11 card tests:
- HPACK
- odd and even stream identifiers that are never reused
- 101 Switching Protocols and Upgrade being unsupported in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (Section 8.6 and the note in Section 8.2.2, the only place the deck may test this)

- **01 (500 fulfills, false).** MDN Window/fetch (Dec 16, 2025): "A fetch() promise does not reject if the server responds with HTTP status codes that indicate errors (404, 504, etc.)". The same-origin wording correctly avoids a CORS failure.
- **02 (ok for 200-299, true).** Fetch: "An ok status is a status in the range 200 to 299, inclusive." MDN Response/ok says the same.

- **04 (credentials default same-origin, true).** MDN Request/credentials: "same-origin ... This is the default."
- **05 (only-if-cached needs cors, false).** Fetch Request constructor: "If request's cache mode is "only-if-cached" and request's mode is not "same-origin", then throw a TypeError." MDN Request/cache agrees. This does not duplicate sr8-05, which is about the RFC 9111 request directive and its 504.
- **06 (If-Match turns default into no-store, true).** HTTP-network-or-cache fetch: "If httpRequest's cache mode is "default" and httpRequest's header list contains If-Modified-Since, If-None-Match, If-Unmodified-Since, If-Match, or If-Range, then set httpRequest's cache mode to "no-store"."
- **07 (GET body with server support, false).** Fetch Request constructor: "... request's method is GET or HEAD, then throw a TypeError." It does not duplicate sr2-05, which is RFC-layer.
- **08 (URL credentials throw TypeError, true).** Fetch: "If parsedURL includes credentials, then throw a TypeError". MDN Request(): "The URL has credentials, such as http://user:password (at) example.com". It does not duplicate sr1-12 (userinfo deprecation).

The spec also says "half" is the only valid value. Watch item, not flagged: MDN Request/duplex (July 3, 2026) marks the feature Experimental and "not Baseline". If the deck wants this card to hold beyond the spec, add "In the Fetch Standard," and consider volatility "may_change".
- **11 (Headers.get() returns an array, false).** MDN Headers/get example returns "deflate, gzip". The Fetch Standard joins values with ", " in list order.
- **12 (patch uppercased, false).** Fetch normalize step uppercases only DELETE, GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, POST and PUT. The spec adds: "Using `patch` is highly likely to result in a `405 Method Not Allowed`."

RFC 7838 §3.1: Caching Alt-Svc Header Field Values

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 recipient rejects an uppercase field name as malformed, so the card must pin the version. RFC 9110 §5.1: "Field names are case-insensitive".
rewrite.statement: In HTTP/1.1, a recipient treats the field names Content-Type and content-type as the same field.
rewrite.explanation: RFC 9110 defines field names as case-insensitive, so an HTTP/1.1 recipient matches Content-Type whatever its capitalization.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: the old wording mixed up http/https with host case, and RFC 9110 allows simple string comparison. Reworded to what the RFC states, that equivalent URIs "can be assumed to identify the same resource" and "The scheme and host are case-insensitive". The answer changes to true because a false 'identify different resources' would add another 'different' false tell. r1 becomes 5T/4F.
rewrite.statement: RFC 9110 lets a recipient assume http URIs whose hosts differ only in letter case identify the same resource.
rewrite.explanation: Scheme and host are case-insensitive in http and https URIs, and URIs that are equivalent after normalization can be assumed to identify the same resource.

rewrite.reason: tell: removes the false-leaning 'classifies X as' template and the word 'different'. The fact (idempotence ignores differing responses) and the answer (false) are unchanged.
rewrite.statement: A DELETE whose repeat gets 404 after a first 204 counts as non-idempotent under RFC 9110.
rewrite.explanation: DELETE stays idempotent even when a repeated request gets a different response, such as 404 after 204. Idempotence concerns the intended effect on the server, not identical status codes.
rewrite.misconception: A method is idempotent only if repeating it returns the same status code.

rewrite.reason: tell: after the r3 drops, true statements averaged 10 characters shorter than false ones. This lengthens the shortest true card without changing its fact (401 carries WWW-Authenticate) or its answer (true). r3 is now T 82.0 vs F 84.0.
rewrite.statement: An origin server sending 401 Unauthorized includes a WWW-Authenticate field in that response.
rewrite.explanation: A server generating 401 must include a WWW-Authenticate challenge applicable to the target resource.

rewrite.reason: tell: removes the 'treats X as a different Y' template, the strongest false tell. The fact (media type tokens are case-insensitive, RFC 9110 §8.3.1) and the answer (false) are unchanged.
rewrite.statement: A recipient matches media type names such as Text/HTML and text/html case-sensitively.
rewrite.explanation: Media type names are case-insensitive: changing the case of the type or subtype leaves the media type unchanged.
rewrite.misconception: Media type names are case-sensitive, so Text/HTML and text/html differ.

rewrite.reason: tell: removes the 'treats X as an instruction to' sub-template and the word 'different'. The fact (Content-Location is metadata, not a redirect; RFC 9110 §8.7) and the answer (false) are unchanged.
rewrite.statement: A user agent follows a response's Content-Location field by requesting that URI.
rewrite.explanation: Content-Location identifies a resource corresponding to the enclosed representation. The field is metadata, rather than a redirect instruction.
rewrite.misconception: Content-Location works like Location and makes the user agent fetch another URI.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: the card described what an origin server does (many really fall back to English). Reworded to what the request means. RFC 9110 §12.4.1: "a request that does not contain the field implies that the sender has no preference on that dimension".
rewrite.statement: Under RFC 9110, a request that omits Accept-Language signals a preference for English.
rewrite.explanation: RFC 9110 says a request lacking a content negotiation field, such as Accept-Language, implies that the sender has no preference on that dimension.
rewrite.misconception: A request without Accept-Language means the client prefers English.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: the statement dropped the condition that must-understand accompanies no-store, and it paraphrased the RFC. RFC 9111 §5.2.2.3: "A response that contains the must-understand directive SHOULD also contain the no-store directive. When a cache that implements the must-understand directive receives a response that includes it, the cache SHOULD ignore the no-store directive if it understands and implements the status code's caching requirements." The verifier's version dropped 'implements must-understand' from the actor, so I restored it.
rewrite.statement: A cache that implements `must-understand` and the status code's caching rules should ignore an accompanying `no-store`.
rewrite.explanation: RFC 9111 has senders pair must-understand with no-store, so caches lacking that support store nothing, while a cache meeting both conditions should ignore no-store.

rewrite.reason: weak_card, rewritten instead of dropped: dropping all four weak r8 cards (03, 07, 10, 11) would leave 8 cards. The old card tied immutable to Authorization, which the prompt forbids. The replacement tests the r8-scoped RFC 8246 limit. RFC 8246 §2: "The immutable extension only applies during the freshness lifetime of the stored response. Stale responses SHOULD be revalidated as they normally would be in the absence of the immutable extension." I avoided 'lets' and 'even after', both false-leaning tells.
rewrite.statement: Under RFC 8246, a client honoring `immutable` skips revalidation once the stored response is stale.
rewrite.explanation: RFC 8246 limits immutable to the stored response's freshness lifetime: once that response is stale, a client should revalidate it as it would without immutable.
rewrite.misconception: immutable means a stored response never needs revalidation, even after it goes stale.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: the statement pinned the server version but not the request version, and an HTTP/1.0 request may omit Host. RFC 9112 §3.2: "A server MUST respond with a 400 (Bad Request) status code to any HTTP/1.1 request message that lacks a Host header field and to any request message that contains more than one Host header field line or a Host header field with an invalid field value." I also removed the vague 'target URI appears elsewhere' from the explanation.
rewrite.statement: A server answers an HTTP/1.1 request that omits the Host field with 400 Bad Request.
rewrite.explanation: RFC 9112 makes a server send 400 for any HTTP/1.1 request that lacks Host, and for any request with more than one Host field line or an invalid Host value.

rewrite.reason: tell: removes the 'treats X as the new Y' template and the word 'new'. The fact (Alt-Svc leaves the origin unchanged) and the answer (false) are unchanged. The source also moves from rfc7838.txt to the HTML section anchor. RFC 7838 §2: "Alternative services do not replace or change the origin for any given resource".
rewrite.statement: A client using Alt-Svc switches the resource's origin to the alternative service's host.
rewrite.explanation: Alt-Svc changes the connection route while the URI's original scheme, host and port continue to identify the resource's origin.
rewrite.misconception: Using an alternative service moves the resource to a new origin at the alternative's host.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: Firefox and Safari stringify a ReadableStream body and send no preflight, so the card is pinned to the Fetch Standard. Fetch (Last Updated 6 October 2026): "The use-CORS-preflight flag is set if ... a ReadableStream object is used in a request", and the Request constructor step: "If this's request's mode is neither "same-origin" nor "cors", then throw a TypeError. Set this's request's use-CORS-preflight flag." Set volatility to may_change (browser support).
rewrite.statement: In the Fetch Standard, a cross-origin fetch() POST with a ReadableStream body goes through CORS preflight.
rewrite.explanation: A ReadableStream request body sets the request's use-CORS-preflight flag, so a cross-origin request is preflighted even with a safelisted method and headers.

rewrite.reason: wrong_answer: as worded ('a browser can'), the statement is true in practice. MDN BCD http.headers.Access-Control-Allow-Headers.authorization_not_covered_by_wildcard, which I checked myself, lists Chrome, Edge and Safari as version_added false, and Firefox 115 only behind a preference. The replacement is pinned to the spec and confirmed. Fetch: "A CORS non-wildcard request-header name is a header name that is a byte-case-insensitive match for `Authorization`", and CORS-preflight fetch: "If one of request's header list's names is a CORS non-wildcard request-header name and is not a byte-case-insensitive match for an item in headerNames, then return a network error." I avoided 'lets', a false tell. Set appliesTo to Fetch Standard and volatility to may_change.
rewrite.statement: In the Fetch Standard, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *` covers the Authorization request header.
rewrite.explanation: The Fetch Standard makes Authorization a CORS non-wildcard request-header name, so a preflight passes only when Access-Control-Allow-Headers names it explicitly.
rewrite.misconception: A * in Access-Control-Allow-Headers covers every request header, Authorization included.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Fetch Standard: CORS non-wildcard request-header name

edits.notes:
I read the prompt's DECK, SECTIONS, RULES and trap lists, and every card in b1 to b4. I confirmed each rewrite and source change against text I fetched today: RFC 9110, 9111, 9112, 8246, 7838 and 9213 from rfc-editor.org (the .html anchors section-1.2, 2.2, 2, 3.1 and RFC 8246 section-2 return 200 and exist), and the Fetch Standard ("Last Updated 6 October 2026"). I also checked MDN BCD for the Authorization wildcard.

Drops versus rewrites:
- All weak, out-of-scope and strawman flags are dropped, except in r8. Dropping all four weak r8 cards would leave 8, so sr8-11 is rewritten to the RFC 8246 freshness-lifetime limit. That card also replaces one that broke the prompt's rule against tying immutable to Authorization.
- r1 and r3 end at exactly 9 cards. r12 ends at 4T/6F, which is the limit but not worse.

Ambiguous and wrong-answer cards:
- sr1-05, sr5-08, sr8-09, sr10-02, sr13-06 and sr13-11 are rewritten.
- sr1-11 flips to true. The false version needed 'different', which is already a false-only tell 7 to 0. The true version adds a true 'lets', against a false-only lead of 3 to 0.
- The sr8-09 rewrite keeps 'implements must-understand' in the actor. The verifier's version dropped it, and that would have made the card wrong for caches that lack must-understand.

Tell rewrites (5): sr2-02, sr5-01, sr5-04 and sr12-09 break the 'treats/classifies X as (a different/new) Y' false template and the 'different/new' tell. sr3-06 is lengthened because the r3 drops left true statements averaging 10 characters shorter than false ones. Each keeps its fact and answer.

Metadata the rewrite schema cannot carry:
- sr13-06 and sr13-11: set appliesTo "Fetch Standard" and volatility "may_change". The volatilityNote should say that MDN compatibility data shows browsers differ: only Chromium supports ReadableStream request bodies, and no shipping browser enforces the Authorization non-wildcard rule by default.
- sr8-11: set appliesTo "RFC 8246", and update its factKey (for example immutable-freshness-lifetime-only).
- sr8-09 and sr10-02: keep their factKeys.

Conflict groups:
- Removed groups left with only one card: get-request-body, interim-vs-final-response, proxy-connection-field-handling, created-201.
- Added field-name-case-by-version (sr1-05 now pins HTTP/1.1, which hints that HTTP/2 differs, as sr11-03 tests).
- Added readablestream-request-body (sr13-06 and sr14-10).

Source changes:
- sr1-01 to RFC 9110 §1.2.
- sr8-12 to the rfc9213.html §2.2 anchor.
- sr12-10 to rfc7838.html §2; sr12-09 gets the same anchor inside its rewrite.
- sr12-11 and sr12-12 to rfc7838.html §3.1.

Open items for the next pass, not edited:
- sr14-10 (duplex required for a stream body) has the same spec-versus-browser gap as sr13-06. It should probably say 'In the Fetch Standard' and be may_change.
- The drops leave coverage gaps worth refilling in a later batch:
  - r3: 403 versus 404, Expect: 100-continue, 201 with no Location falling back to the target URI.
  - r8: request max-age with max-stale, proxy-revalidate alone not making a response cacheable, stale-if-error and a visibly stale Age.
  - r11: 101 and Upgrade unsupported in HTTP/2, one connection per host and port.
  - r12: why QPACK replaced HPACK, TLS 1.3 as the minimum for QUIC.
  - r1: the tunnel as a blind relay.
  The verifiers' suggested texts for these are usable once checked.
- sr4-04 and sr7-04 share the true template 'A cache classifies <code> as heuristically cacheable'. They are different facts, so I left them.

cards.statement: In HTTP/1.1, a recipient treats the field names Content-Type and content-type as the same field.
cards.explanation: RFC 9110 defines field names as case-insensitive, so an HTTP/1.1 recipient matches Content-Type whatever its capitalization.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Checked RFC 9110 §5.1 myself: "Field names are case-insensitive". Pinning to HTTP/1.1 avoids the HTTP/2 lowercase rule, which is tested separately in r11.

cards.statement: RFC 9110 lets a recipient assume http URIs whose hosts differ only in letter case identify the same resource.
cards.explanation: Scheme and host are case-insensitive in http and https URIs, and URIs that are equivalent after normalization can be assumed to identify the same resource.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Checked RFC 9110 §4.2.3 myself: "The scheme and host are case-insensitive" and "Two HTTP URIs that are equivalent after normalization (using any method) can be assumed to identify the same resource". Section r1 still has hedges on both true and false cards.

cards.statement: A DELETE whose repeat gets 404 after a first 204 counts as non-idempotent under RFC 9110.
cards.explanation: DELETE stays idempotent even when a repeated request gets a different response, such as 404 after 204. Idempotence concerns the intended effect on the server, not identical status codes.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Checked RFC 9110 §9.2.2 myself: DELETE is listed as idempotent, and the RFC says "the same intended effect, even if the original request succeeded, though the response might differ". The explanation is 186 characters.

cards.statement: An origin server sending 401 Unauthorized includes a WWW-Authenticate field in that response.
cards.explanation: A server generating 401 must include a WWW-Authenticate challenge applicable to the target resource.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Checked RFC 9110 §15.5.2 myself: "The server generating a 401 response MUST send a WWW-Authenticate header field", so the 'must' in the explanation matches the RFC's MUST.

cards.statement: A recipient matches media type names such as Text/HTML and text/html case-sensitively.
cards.explanation: Media type names are case-insensitive: changing the case of the type or subtype leaves the media type unchanged.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Checked RFC 9110 §8.3.1 myself: "The type and subtype tokens are case-insensitive." The statement covers names only, so the case rules for parameter values do not come into it.

cards.statement: A user agent follows a response's Content-Location field by requesting that URI.
cards.explanation: Content-Location identifies a resource corresponding to the enclosed representation. The field is metadata, rather than a redirect instruction.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Checked RFC 9110 §8.7 myself: "The Content-Location value is not a replacement for the target URI ... It is representation metadata."

cards.statement: Under RFC 9110, a request that omits Accept-Language signals a preference for English.
cards.explanation: RFC 9110 says a request lacking a content negotiation field, such as Accept-Language, implies that the sender has no preference on that dimension.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Checked RFC 9110 §12.4.1 myself: a request that does not contain the field "implies that the sender has no preference on that dimension of negotiation".

cards.statement: A cache that implements `must-understand` and the status code's caching rules should ignore an accompanying `no-store`.
cards.explanation: RFC 9111 has senders pair must-understand with no-store, so caches lacking that support store nothing, while a cache meeting both conditions should ignore no-store.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Checked RFC 9111 §5.2.2.3 myself: "SHOULD also contain the no-store directive ... the cache SHOULD ignore the no-store directive if it understands and implements the status code's caching requirements." The statement is 119 characters and the explanation 164.

cards.statement: Under RFC 8246, a client honoring `immutable` skips revalidation once the stored response is stale.
cards.explanation: RFC 8246 limits immutable to the stored response's freshness lifetime: once that response is stale, a client should revalidate it as it would without immutable.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Checked RFC 8246 §2 myself: "only applies during the freshness lifetime of the stored response. Stale responses SHOULD be revalidated". The card no longer ties immutable to Authorization.

cards.statement: A server answers an HTTP/1.1 request that omits the Host field with 400 Bad Request.
cards.explanation: RFC 9112 makes a server send 400 for any HTTP/1.1 request that lacks Host, and for any request with more than one Host field line or an invalid Host value.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Checked RFC 9112 §3.2 myself: "A server MUST respond with a 400 (Bad Request) status code to any HTTP/1.1 request message that lacks a Host header field and to any request message that contains more than one Host header field line or a Host header field with an invalid field value."

cards.statement: A client using Alt-Svc switches the resource's origin to the alternative service's host.
cards.explanation: Alt-Svc changes the connection route while the URI's original scheme, host and port continue to identify the resource's origin.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Checked RFC 7838 §2 myself: "Alternative services do not replace or change the origin for any given resource".

cards.statement: In the Fetch Standard, a cross-origin fetch() POST with a ReadableStream body goes through CORS preflight.
cards.explanation: A ReadableStream request body sets the request's use-CORS-preflight flag, so a cross-origin request is preflighted even with a safelisted method and headers.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Checked the Fetch Standard (Last Updated 6 October 2026) myself: "The use-CORS-preflight flag is set if ... a ReadableStream object is used in a request", the Request constructor step "Set this's request's use-CORS-preflight flag", and HTTP fetch runs a CORS-preflight fetch when the flag is set. A cached preflight entry is a narrow edge that does not flip the answer. Volatility stays may_change.

cards.statement: In the Fetch Standard, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *` covers the Authorization request header.
cards.explanation: The Fetch Standard makes Authorization a CORS non-wildcard request-header name, so a preflight passes only when Access-Control-Allow-Headers names it explicitly.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep. Checked the Fetch Standard myself: "A CORS non-wildcard request-header name is a header name that is a byte-case-insensitive match for `Authorization`", and CORS-preflight fetch returns a network error if that name is not matched by an item in headerNames, whatever the credentials mode. Pinning the card to the spec avoids engine differences, and volatility stays may_change.
